Espouse

/ih-SPOWZ/ - rhymes with vows · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Espouse means to take up and publicly support a cause.

The chef has espoused nose-to-tail cooking since her first restaurant, printing the philosophy right on the menu.

Worked Example

Nobody expected the quiet cartographer to espouse open data. But when the county tried to lock its maps behind fees, she gave talks, wrote letters, and put her name on the lawsuit — the cause was publicly hers from then on.

Espouse is stronger than support and more public than believe in: you take the cause up as your own and say so where it costs you something. The word began as 'to marry' — and a trace of the wedding survives: espousing a cause means being joined to it in front of witnesses.

How Espouse Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

embrace

embrace: to take a cause to heart — you can embrace an idea privately; espousing is public

uphold

uphold: to defend something already established; espouse often takes up the new or the out-of-favor

Antonyms

renounce

renounce: to give a cause up formally and publicly

oppose

oppose: to work against it

How Strong Is It? — applaud → espouse → crusade

applaud vs. espouse

applaud vs. espouse: Applauding a cause costs one evening and both hands — approval from a seat in the audience, nothing pledged.

crusade vs. espouse

crusade vs. espouse: Crusade goes further than espouse — the espoused cause has your name and your voice, but a crusade takes the rest of the calendar too.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — espouse

Root — espouse: to pledge, to wed — from Old French espouser, Latin spondere 'to pledge'

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off in English — espouse came over whole from Old French espouser, 'to wed.' Behind it stands Latin spondere, 'to make a solemn pledge,' the Romans' word for betrothals. Marry the idea, then: to espouse a cause is to wed yourself to it, publicly and on the record, the way sponsors and spouses — the root's other children — are bound by their word.

Use the root in a new word: sponsor

Use the root in a new word: sponsor: The hardware store agreed to sponsor the relay team and stood by them through a losing season.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / public

Espouse belongs to public life: causes, doctrines, reforms — things you adopt and argue for where it shows. Support is milder, and embrace can stay private. One warning: despite the wedding in its history, modern English does not use espouse for marrying — a sentence about espousing a person will read as a mistake.
